scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Pungmul originated in Korea’s agrarian society as a form of collective labor music and shamanistic ritual accompaniment.
Historically called nongak, the term was imposed during Japanese colonial rule (1910–1945) to restrict its meaning.
The tradition was suppressed under Japanese occupation due to its potential to mobilize communities.
on_screen: Map: South Korea · East Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Pungmul was traditionally performed during farming work, village festivals, shamanistic rituals, and community events.
It served to motivate labor, bless crops, and expel evil spirits.
In modern times, it has been used in pro-democracy protests and as a performing art.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The core percussion instruments are kkwaenggwari (small handheld gong), janggu (hourglass drum), buk (barrel drum), and jing (large gong).
Wind instruments like taepyeongso sometimes accompany the ensemble.
Listen for the kkwaenggwari, janggu, buk, jing.
The pulse is varies; includes 12-beat gutgeori, 9/8 semachi, 4/4 or 12/8 hwimori, and fast 12/8 jajinmori.

A vibrant, layered percussion ensemble featuring sharp metallic strikes of the kkwaenggwari, deep resonant beats of the buk and jing, and intricate rhythms of the janggu, punctuated by lively wind instrument flourishes and energetic vocal chants.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear colorful costumes, often including a floral version of the Buddhist gokkal head-dress.
Advanced performers wear sangmo hats with long ribbons spun in intricate patterns.
Japsaek actors dress as caricatures of traditional village roles.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Kim Duk-soo and Kim Yong-bae are key figures who pioneered the modern SamulNori style by adapting pungmul for stage performance in 1978.
Architect Kim Swoo Geun designed the Konggansarang performance hall where this transformation occurred.
South Korea recognizes five regional pungmul styles: Jinju Samcheonpo (South Gyeongsang), Pyeongtaek (Gyeonggi), Iri (North Jeolla), Gangneung (Gangwon), and Imsil Pilbong (North Jeolla).
Pungmul evolved from ancient Korean agrarian and shamanistic traditions.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Pungmul is child of Samulnori: Modern staged percussion genre derived from pungmul’s core instruments and rhythms.
Pungmul is shares music of Namsadang: Itinerant performance troupe that includes pungmul in its repertoire.
Pungmul is sibling of Pung cholom: A similar dance from Manipur, India, sharing percussion and dance elements.
